sources.indigo_citation: Carole Goldberg, Tribal Jurisdictional Status Analysis (Tribal Court Clearinghouse, updated Feb. 16, 2010)
sources.title: Carole Goldberg, Tribal Jurisdictional Status Analysis, Tribal Court Clearinghouse (updated 2010)
sources.how_read: Read footnotes 1-5 of the page. Secondary source used only to corroborate; it contains at least one date I could not confirm (it dates Nevada's assumption to 1967 and the Statutes show 1955).

facts.detail: Since April 11, 1968, a state that did not already have criminal jurisdiction in Indian country may assume it only with the consent of the tribe occupying the affected Indian country. (25 U.S.C. § 1321(a)(1).)
facts.quote: to assume, with the consent of the Indian tribe occupying the particular Indian country or part thereof which could be affected by such assumption
facts.note: General rule, not tied to one nation. Enacted as Pub. L. 90-284, tit. IV, § 401, 82 Stat. 78 (1968); subsec. (a)(2) added in 2010.

facts.detail: Since April 11, 1968, a state that did not already have civil jurisdiction over causes of action in Indian country may assume it only with the consent of the tribe occupying the affected Indian country. (25 U.S.C. § 1322(a).)
facts.quote: to assume, with the consent of the tribe occupying the particular Indian country or part thereof which would be affected by such assumption
facts.note: General rule. Pub. L. 90-284, tit. IV, § 402, 82 Stat. 79 (1968).

facts.detail: State jurisdiction acquired under the 1968 amendments applies in Indian country only if the enrolled Indians of the affected area accept it by majority vote of adults voting at a special election called by the Secretary of the Interior. (25 U.S.C. § 1326.)
facts.quote: accept such jurisdiction by a majority vote of the adult Indians voting at a special election held for that purpose
facts.note: The Secretary calls the election when requested by the tribal council or by 20 percent of enrolled adults (same section). Utah and North Dakota statutes already recorded rely on this.

facts.detail: The United States may accept a state's retrocession of all or part of the criminal or civil jurisdiction the state acquired under Public Law 280. (25 U.S.C. § 1323(a).)
facts.quote: The United States is authorized to accept a retrocession by any State of all or any measure of the criminal or civil jurisdiction, or both

facts.detail: Section 7 of Public Law 280, the provision that let a state assume jurisdiction by its own legislation without tribal consent, was repealed in 1968, but earlier assumptions were left intact. (25 U.S.C. § 1323(b).)
facts.quote: is hereby repealed, but such repeal shall not affect any cession of jurisdiction made pursuant to such section prior to its repeal
facts.note: Section 7 of the Act of Aug. 15, 1953, 67 Stat. 588. The Eighth Circuit read the repeal as ending nonconsensual assumptions "at any time and in any manner after 1968" (Rosebud, 900 F.2d at 1172).

facts.detail: Arizona enacted A.R.S. §§ 36-1801 and 36-1865 under Public Law 280, applying its air and water pollution laws to all Indian lands with civil and criminal enforcement on reservations; that is the only subject-matter assumption BIA lists for Arizona. (Francisco v. State, 113 Ariz. 427, 430 n.2 (1976).)
facts.quote: its air and water pollution abatement laws will apply to all Indian lands
facts.note: BIA dates the Arizona assumption to 1967. I could not read the 1967 session law (azmemory.azlibrary.gov blocked); Goldberg cites "Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 36-1801, 36-1856 (1973 Supp.)" (36-1856 vs. the court's 36-1865; I follow the court). Applies to every Arizona reservation by its terms but only for pollution control.

facts.detail: A.R.S. § 36-1801 (state jurisdiction over air pollution on Indian lands) was recodified as § 49-561 in 1986 and is no longer in Arizona law; EPA treated the assumption as inconsistent with federal law. (81 Fed. Reg. 7209, 7211 (Feb. 11, 2016).)
facts.quote: ARS section 36–1801 was recodified as ARS section 49–561 in 1986, but is no longer found in Arizona law.
facts.note: Confirmed that A.R.S. § 49-561 returns "page not found" on azleg.gov while neighbouring § 49-551 loads. I could not read the repealing session laws. Goldberg (2010) says water-pollution assumption was repealed by Ariz. Laws 1986 § 19(B) and air by Ariz. Laws 2003 § 4; Laws 2003 ch. 4 is a community-college bill, so her citation is unverified. Status of the water-pollution section (36-1865) is from Goldberg only.

facts.detail: Apart from the repealed pollution statutes, Arizona has not assumed civil or criminal jurisdiction over Indian reservations; the Arizona Supreme Court held the State has no authority to extend its laws to an Indian reservation. (Francisco v. State, 113 Ariz. 427, 431 (1976).)
facts.quote: Arizona has no authority to extend the application of its laws to an Indian reservation
facts.note: 1976 holding about service of process on the Tohono O'odham (Papago) reservation, reasoning from the 1968 consent requirement. I did not find any later Arizona assumption. Other federal statutes can still give Arizona limited authority; none checked here.

facts.detail: South Dakota's 1957 act (S.D. Codified Laws §§ 1-1-12 to 1-1-16) offered to assume civil and criminal jurisdiction if the affected tribes consented; the Eighth Circuit found consent was not given, so jurisdiction was never assumed under it. (Rosebud Sioux Tribe v. South Dakota, 900 F.2d 1164, 1166 (8th Cir. 1990).)
facts.quote: Since tribal consent was not given, jurisdiction was never assumed under this law.
facts.note: Section 1-1-13 says a tribe that took no action within one year of Oct. 1, 1957 is deemed to consent; the court nevertheless held consent was not given. The sections are still printed in the code. The related 1959 highway statute (§ 1-1-17) also never took effect because its condition (roads jointly maintained by State and United States) was never met (900 F.2d at 1166). Shakopee, Northern Cheyenne and Turtle Mountain have only trust-land presence in SD in the roster and are not mapped.

facts.detail: South Dakota's 1961 act (S.D. Codified Laws §§ 1-1-18 to 1-1-21) declared a general assumption of jurisdiction in Indian country, but it takes effect only on a gubernatorial proclamation, which was never issued; the general assumption never occurred. (S.D. Codified Laws § 1-1-21; 900 F.2d at 1167.)
facts.locator: S.D. Codified Laws § 1-1-21 (SL 1961, ch. 464, § 4); 900 F.2d at 1167
facts.quote: The general assumption of jurisdiction did not occur since the Governor of South Dakota never filed the required proclamation.
facts.note: Quote is from Rosebud. A 1963 attempt to assume full jurisdiction (1963 S.D. Laws ch. 467) was defeated 3 to 1 in a referendum (900 F.2d at 1167). Statute text in § 1-1-21: highways are excepted from the proclamation requirement.

facts.detail: South Dakota's 1961 highway-only assumption was held invalid by the South Dakota Supreme Court in 1964 (In re Hankins) and, after that court revived it in State v. Onihan (1988), by the Eighth Circuit in 1990: without tribal consent the State has no civil or criminal jurisdiction over highways through Indian lands. (Rosebud, 900 F.2d at 1166-67, 1172.)
facts.quote: Absent tribal consent, we hold the State of South Dakota has no jurisdiction over the highways running through Indian lands in the state.
facts.note: Hankins: 80 S.D. 435, 442-43, 125 N.W.2d 839, 842-43 (state cannot assume jurisdiction over highways alone; the Eighth Circuit describes this at 900 F.2d at 1167). Rosebud's further holding (at 1170-72): the highway-only scheme does not meet Public Law 280, and the 1968 consent requirement bars later nonconsensual assumption. Cert. history not checked. Parties: Rosebud, Cheyenne River, Oglala, Standing Rock; the holding is about "Indian lands in the state" generally.

facts.detail: Today South Dakota holds no Public Law 280 jurisdiction over any of its reservations: the 1957 act was never consented to, the 1961 general act never took effect, and the 1961 highway piece is invalid; the statutes stay in the code. (Rosebud, 900 F.2d at 1166-67; S.D. Codified Laws §§ 1-1-12 to 1-1-21.)
facts.quote: the provisions of chapter 106 of the Session Laws of the State of South Dakota for 1901, as amended, or any law to the contrary, notwithstanding, the State of South Dakota assumes and accepts jurisdiction
facts.note: Quote is the 1957 assumption text, § 1-1-12, shown because it is still printed in the code. Conclusion that nothing is in force is mine, drawn from Rosebud (1990) plus the statutes; I did not find any later tribal consent election or any post-1990 South Dakota assumption. Goldberg (2010) fn. 4 reaches the same view.

facts.detail: North Dakota's ch. 27-19 extends state civil jurisdiction over a reservation only on acceptance by its Indian citizens, and the Legislative Council staff reported in 2004 that no tribe had voted to consent after 1968. (N.D. Legis. Council Memo. 59215, at 3 (2004).)
facts.quote: Since the enactment of this amendment, no tribe has voted to consent to state court jurisdiction.
facts.note: Secondary source (legislative staff memo, 2004); I have no later source. "This amendment" is the 1968 consent amendment. The 1946 Devils Lake act (separate fact) is a separate criminal grant.

facts.detail: The Supreme Court recorded that the Three Affiliated Tribes had not consented to state-court jurisdiction over Fort Berthold under ch. 27-19, so North Dakota had not assumed civil jurisdiction there. (Three Affiliated Tribes v. Wold Eng'g, 467 U.S. 138, 145 (1984).)
facts.quote: Because the petitioner Tribe at no point has consented to state-court jurisdiction under Chapter 27-19 over the Fort Berthold Reservation
facts.note: Wold II (476 U.S. 877, 881) repeats the point; Wold II held ch. 27-19 pre-empted insofar as it disclaims pre-existing state jurisdiction over a tribe's suit against a non-Indian with no other forum, absent waiver of immunity. Wold I dissent (Rehnquist, J., 467 U.S. at 162) says "North Dakota has not assumed any additional jurisdiction over Indian country under Pub. L. 280."

facts.detail: A 1946 act conferred on North Dakota jurisdiction over offenses by or against Indians on the Devils Lake (now Spirit Lake) Reservation to the same extent as elsewhere in the State, without ousting federal courts. (Act of May 31, 1946, ch. 279, 60 Stat. 229.)
facts.quote: by or against Indians on the Devils Lake Indian Reservation in North Dakota to the same extent as its courts have jurisdiction generally over offenses committed within said State
facts.note: Criminal only. The Senate report (S. Rep. 116-130 at 2) identifies the Devils Lake Reservation as the Spirit Lake Reservation. Not codified in the U.S. Code.

facts.detail: Congress has not repealed the 1946 act. Repeal bills in the 115th (S. 2788) and 116th (S. 2159, H.R. 3831) Congresses were reported by the Senate committee or referred, and not enacted; I found no public law repealing it through the 119th Congress listing. (S. Rep. No. 116-130, at 2 (2019).)
facts.quote: On July 24, 2019, S. 2159 was reported favorably without amendment.
facts.note: "Not repealed" rests on absence: the Congress.gov API list of enacted laws for the 116th-119th Congresses (checked 2026-11-23; 119th list showed 144 laws) contains no repeal; govinfo BILLSTATUS for S. 2159 ends 2019-10-16 (placed on calendar) and for H.R. 3831 at 2019-08-02 (committee referral). I did not find a 117th-119th Congress repeal bill. Verify before publishing.

facts.detail: Montana's 2024 legislative staff summary states that the Flathead Reservation is the only reservation in Montana under Public Law 280; no other Montana reservation is under state jurisdiction by the 1963 act. (Mont. Legis. Servs. Div., Montana & Public Law 280, at 1 (Apr. 2024).)
facts.locator: Mont. Legis. Servs. Div. memo p. 1; Mont. Code Ann. § 2-1-301
facts.quote: The only reservation in Montana under PL-280 is the Flathead Reservation.
facts.note: Secondary source (legislative staff). Statutory text names only Flathead in § 2-1-301. Little Shell has no reservation in the roster data. Turtle Mountain (ND-based) has MT presence only. Fort Peck: a state court allowed divorce under a 1938 tribal enactment (State ex rel. Iron Bear v. Dist. Ct., 162 Mont. 335, 512 P.2d 1292 (1973)); that is tribal consent in a domestic-relations setting, not Public Law 280; I read only the opening.

facts.detail: The Supreme Court held that Montana never took the "affirmative legislative action" needed to assume jurisdiction over the Blackfeet Reservation, so a tribal-council act could not give the State civil jurisdiction. (Kennerly v. Dist. Ct. of Mont., 400 U.S. 423, 425, 427 (1971).)
facts.quote: But Montana never took "affirmative legislative action"-concerning either civil or criminal jurisdiction-with respect to the Blackfeet Reservation.
facts.note: Quote as printed in the official report (dash punctuation as in the PDF text). Holding at 427: the Tribal Council's unilateral action was insufficient under the 1953 Act.

facts.detail: Montana law lets any other tribe request state jurisdiction by resolution to the governor, who must proclaim it within 60 days, but only after the tribe's own approval and the consent of each affected county commission. (Mont. Code Ann. § 2-1-302.)
facts.quote: a resolution expressing its desire that its people and lands be subject to the criminal or civil jurisdiction, or both, of the state
facts.note: Procedure only; I found no proclamation under it for any other tribe. Under § 2-1-303 the State assumes jurisdiction 60 days after the proclamation. Enacted as 1963 Mont. Laws ch. 81 (section history lines).

facts.detail: Congress conferred on Kansas jurisdiction over offenses committed by or against Indians on Indian reservations in Kansas, including trust or restricted allotments, to the same extent as elsewhere in the State; federal courts keep jurisdiction over federal offenses. (18 U.S.C. § 3243.)
facts.quote: Jurisdiction is conferred on the State of Kansas over offenses committed by or against Indians on Indian reservations, including trust or restricted allotments
facts.note: Criminal only; no civil grant. The four roster entries list KS because of reservation or trust-land presence in Kansas (Iowa Tribe and Sac and Fox of Missouri straddle KS/NE).

facts.detail: New York has jurisdiction over offenses committed by or against Indians on Indian reservations in the State, to the same extent as elsewhere in the State; treaty hunting and fishing rights are preserved. (25 U.S.C. § 232.)
facts.quote: The State of New York shall have jurisdiction over offenses committed by or against Indians on Indian reservations within the State of New York
facts.note: Applies to "Indian reservations within the State of New York." Whether particular parcels (for example Oneida, Cayuga or Shinnecock lands) are "reservations" is a separate question I did not research.

facts.detail: New York courts have jurisdiction over civil actions between Indians or between Indians and others, as in other civil actions, with limits: no state taxation of reservation lands, no state licence for treaty hunting and fishing, and no alienation of tribal land. (25 U.S.C. § 233.)
facts.quote: shall have jurisdiction in civil actions and proceedings between Indians or between one or more Indians and any other person or persons
facts.note: Section 233 also excludes civil actions involving Indian lands or claims about events before Sept. 13, 1952; tribes could preserve their own laws and customs by enactment before Sept. 13, 1952.

facts.detail: The Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act subjects the Passamaquoddy Tribe and Penobscot Nation, their members and lands to Maine's jurisdiction as provided in the Maine Implementing Act, which applies state law and state court jurisdiction to them "except as otherwise provided." (Pub. L. No. 96-420, § 6(b)(1), 94 Stat. at 1794; Me. Rev. Stat. Ann. tit. 30, § 6204.)
facts.quote: shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the State of Maine to the extent and in the manner provided in the Maine Implementing Act
facts.note: The Implementing Act also gives these two nations separate tribal jurisdiction in listed areas (30 M.R.S. §§ 6206, 6209-A, 6209-B; § 6(f) of the federal Act); I read the federal grant and § 6204 only. § 6(c) removes federal criminal jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1152-1153 etc. Maine's 2022-2023 tribal-state legislation was not analyzed. 25 U.S.C. § 1725 is "omitted" from the Code and is cited here as the Statutes at Large section.

facts.detail: Indians and tribes in Maine other than the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot, including the Houlton Band of Maliseets, and their lands are subject to state civil and criminal jurisdiction and state courts as any other person or land, except where the Act provides otherwise. (Pub. L. No. 96-420, § 6(a), 94 Stat. at 1793.)
facts.quote: the civil and criminal jurisdiction of the State, the laws of the State, and the civil and criminal jurisdiction of the courts of the State, to the same extent as any other person or land therein
facts.note: Section 6(e)(2) (94 Stat. at 1794) lets the State and the Band agree on state jurisdiction over Band lands. Section 6(a) is "except as provided in section 8(e) and section 5(d)(4)." Houlton Band is not named in 6(a); it falls in "all other Indians." Section 6(b)(1) names only the two tribes.

facts.detail: Congress treated the Aroostook Band of Micmacs (now Mi'kmaq Nation) like the other Maine tribes under the 1980 settlement act and authorized Maine and the Band to agree on state jurisdiction over Band lands; Maine's 2023 Mi'kmaq Nation Restoration Act gives the Nation exclusive jurisdiction over listed matters. (Pub. L. No. 102-171, § 6(b), (d), 105 Stat. at 1148; Me. Rev. Stat. Ann. tit. 30, § 7208(1).)
facts.quote: The State of Maine and the Band are authorized to execute agreements regarding the jurisdiction of the State of Maine over lands owned by, or held in trust for the benefit of, the Band
facts.note: I did not read the state-law section of the Mi'kmaq Nation Restoration Act that applies general state law (30 M.R.S. § 7204 returned 404), so the extent of residual state jurisdiction is not confirmed. Section 7208(1): "the Mi'kmaq Nation has the right to exercise exclusive jurisdiction, separate and distinct from the State, over" listed matters. Part 3 of the federal act (§ 6(b)) gives the Band and its lands "the same status as other tribes" under the 1980 act.

facts.detail: Settlement lands of the Narragansett Indian Tribe are subject to the civil and criminal laws and jurisdiction of Rhode Island; the First Circuit held this grant valid and covers civil regulatory jurisdiction. (Pub. L. No. 95-395, § 9, 92 Stat. at 817; Rhode Island v. Narragansett Indian Tribe, 19 F.3d 685, 694 (1st Cir. 1994).)
facts.quote: civil and criminal laws and jurisdiction of the State of Rhode Island
facts.note: Applies to "settlement lands"; I did not research later trust acquisitions. The 1996 amendment (Pub. L. 104-208, § 330, 110 Stat. 3009-227) kept the sentence as § 9(a) and added § 9(b), settlement lands are not "Indian lands" for the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. 25 U.S.C. § 1708 is "omitted" from the Code. Whether Narragansett's "civil regulatory" reach holds today was not rechecked beyond the 1994 opinion.

facts.detail: Congress declared the Mashantucket Pequot reservation Indian country subject to Connecticut jurisdiction to the maximum extent provided in title IV of the 1968 Act (the Public Law 280 consent provisions), waiving the special-election requirement of § 406. (Pub. L. No. 98-134, § 6, 97 Stat. at 855.)
facts.quote: the reservation of the Tribe is declared to be Indian country subject to State jurisdiction
facts.note: The statute's sentence continues "to the maximum extent provided in title IV of such Act." 25 U.S.C. § 1755 is "omitted" from the Code. The text layer of this page prints "title I V of s u c h Act" so I stopped the quote earlier.

facts.detail: Congress consented to Connecticut's assumption of criminal jurisdiction over offenses by or against Indians on the Mohegan reservation, without waiving federal jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. § 1153 or ending the Tribe's concurrent jurisdiction. (Pub. L. No. 103-377, § 6, 108 Stat. at 3505.)
facts.quote: the consent of the United States is hereby given to the assumption of jurisdiction by the State of Connecticut over criminal offenses committed by or against Indians on the reservation of the Mohegan Tribe
facts.note: Criminal only. Quote skips the words "Subject to subsection (b)," at the start of § 6(a). 25 U.S.C. § 1775d (omitted from the Code).

facts.detail: Settlement lands and other Indian-held land in the town of Gay Head (Aquinnah) are subject to the civil and criminal laws, ordinances and jurisdiction of Massachusetts and the town, except as the Act or the State Implementing Act expressly provides. (Pub. L. No. 100-95, § 9, 101 Stat. at 709.)
facts.quote: shall be subject to the civil and criminal laws, ordinances, and jurisdiction of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and the town of Gay Head
facts.note: Section 7(a) (101 Stat. at 707) also bars the tribal council from exercising jurisdiction "in contravention of" the Act and Massachusetts criminal and civil regulatory law. 25 U.S.C. § 1771g is "omitted" from the Code. I did not research Aquinnah litigation after 1987. No comparable statute found for the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe.

facts.detail: South Carolina has civil, criminal and regulatory jurisdiction over the Catawba Tribe, its members and lands as over any other person or land, except where the State Act or federal implementing law says otherwise; federal law adopts the Settlement Agreement and State Act for these questions. (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-16-40; Pub. L. No. 103-116, § 10(1), 107 Stat. at 1126.)
facts.quote: is subject to the civil, criminal, and regulatory jurisdiction of the State, its agencies, and political subdivisions other than municipalities
facts.note: Federal side: § 10(1), "All matters involving tribal powers, immunities, and jurisdiction, whether criminal, civil, or regulatory, shall be governed by the terms and provisions of the Settlement Agreement and the State Act." Section 5(e)(?) of the federal Act (107 Stat. at 1122): the Act does not "deprive the State of jurisdiction other than as expressly provided." The State Act also lets the Tribe create tribal courts (S.C. Code Ann. §§ 27-16-110 to -120 not fully read).

facts.detail: Texas exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction within the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo reservation as if it had assumed that jurisdiction with the tribe's consent under 25 U.S.C. §§ 1321 and 1322. (Pub. L. No. 100-89, § 105(f), 101 Stat. 666, 668.)
facts.quote: The State shall exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction within the boundaries of the reservation as if such State had assumed such jurisdiction with the consent of the tribe
facts.note: 25 U.S.C. § 1300g-4 is "omitted" from the Code. Gaming provisions (§ 107) and Ysleta del Sur Pueblo v. Texas, 596 U.S. 685 (2022), were not analyzed.

facts.detail: Texas exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction within the Alabama-Coushatta reservation as if it had assumed that jurisdiction with the tribe's consent under 25 U.S.C. §§ 1321 and 1322. (Pub. L. No. 100-89, § 206(f), 101 Stat. at 671-72.)
facts.quote: The State shall exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction within the boundaries of the reservation as if such State had assumed such jurisdiction with the consent of the tribe
facts.note: Quote sentence is identical to § 105(f); it appears at the bottom of 101 Stat. 671 and top of 672. Codified (as omitted) at 25 U.S.C. § 736.

facts.detail: Texas exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction over the Kickapoo band's trust lands in Maverick County as if it had assumed it under the 1968 Act, and may receive retrocession under § 403. (Pub. L. No. 97-429, § 6, 96 Stat. at 2270.)
facts.quote: The State of Texas shall exercise jurisdiction over civil causes of action and criminal offenses arising on the Band's trust lands
facts.note: 25 U.S.C. § 1300b-15 is "omitted" from the Code. This statute was not on your list; found through the Cornell notes.

facts.detail: Florida's Public Law 280 assumption (Fla. Stat. § 285.16) continues in force on land taken into trust under the Seminole land claims settlement unless the United States accepts retrocession, and Florida alcohol, gambling and cigarette laws also apply there. (Pub. L. No. 100-228, § 6(d)(1), 101 Stat. at 1560.)
facts.quote: the assumption of jurisdiction in favor of the State contained in section 285.16, Florida Statutes
facts.note: Quote is the first part of the clause; it continues "shall continue in full force and effect on such lands unless the United States accepts a retrocession." 25 U.S.C. § 1772d is "omitted" from the Code. The Miccosukee Tribe and Poarch Band: no similar statute found (not researched in depth).

facts.detail: The 1980 restoration act directs Utah to exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over the Paiute reservation and persons on it as if Utah had assumed jurisdiction under Public Law 280, and under Utah Code §§ 63-36-9 to -21 (now Utah Code § 9-9-201 et seq.). (Pub. L. No. 96-227, § 7(b), 94 Stat. at 320.)
facts.quote: The State of Utah shall exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction with respect to the reservation and persons on the reservation as if it had assumed jurisdiction
facts.note: The text refers to the Utah consent statute you already read (special election). I did not determine whether the tribe has voted; Pub. L. 109-126, § 4 (2005) amended the reservation provisions and was not read. Goldberg (2010) lists this under Utah as conferring state jurisdiction. 25 U.S.C. § 766 is "omitted" from the Code. Renumbering 63-36-9 to 9-9-201 is from your earlier reading, not mine.

facts.detail: The 1948 act that gave Iowa criminal jurisdiction over offenses by or against Indians on the Sac and Fox (Meskwaki) Reservation was repealed on Dec. 11, 2018. (Pub. L. No. 115-301, 132 Stat. 4395.)
facts.quote: 1161, chapter 759) is repealed
facts.note: Original grant: Act of June 30, 1948, ch. 759, 62 Stat. 1161, "jurisdiction is hereby conferred on the State of Iowa over offenses committed by or against Indians on the Sac and Fox Indian Reservation in that State" (marginal headnotes interleave in the scan text layer). Iowa civil jurisdiction (Iowa Code § 1.12) was already recorded and is separate.

facts.detail: Mississippi has no Public Law 280 or special-act jurisdiction over Choctaw trust lands that I found; the Supreme Court held that where the Major Crimes Act applies the State has no similar jurisdiction. (United States v. John, 437 U.S. 634, 653 (1978).)
facts.quote: the State has no similar jurisdiction
facts.note: Narrow: John concerns a Major Crimes Act offense (assault with intent to kill) on Choctaw trust land. "Not assumed" for broader civil or criminal matters rests on not finding any grant; I did not find a Mississippi statute assuming jurisdiction. Quote begins mid-sentence in the opinion.

facts.detail: Nevada's 1955 act assumed civil and criminal jurisdiction over Indian country in all counties, unless a county board petitioned the Governor before the effective date (90 days after July 1, 1955) and the Governor excluded that county's Indian country by proclamation. (1955 Nev. Stat. ch. 198, §§ 1-3, at 297.)
facts.quote: the State of Nevada does hereby assume jurisdiction over public offenses committed by or against Indians in the areas of Indian country in Nevada
facts.note: Mapped to the nations whose lands appear in the 1975 and 1988 retrocession notices (see those facts). Odger's Ranch and Ruby Valley Allotment, named in the 1975 notice, are not mapped because I could not tie them to a roster entry. The 1955 act was later folded into NRS 41.430 (history line "1:198:1955").

facts.detail: Since July 1, 1974 NRS 41.430 applies only where the tribe consented, by referendum under sections 6-14 of the 1973 act or under 25 U.S.C. § 1326; where a tribe refused, Nevada "recedes from and relinquishes" jurisdiction. The Indian affairs commission was to hold the referenda by June 4, 1974. (1973 Nev. Stat. ch. 601, §§ 1, 6, at 1051-53; Nev. Rev. Stat. § 41.430(3)-(4).)
facts.quote: the State of Nevada hereby recedes from and relinquishes jurisdiction over any such area
facts.note: Sections 1-5 took effect July 1, 1974 (§ 16). The current NRS text still carries this language. Goldberg (2010) says no tribe asked to continue; the 1976 AIPRC report says Ely Colony alone chose to keep state jurisdiction. Goldberg's date for the assumption (1967) conflicts with the Statutes (1955).

facts.detail: On July 1, 1975 the Bureau of Indian Affairs accepted Nevada's offer to retrocede all civil and criminal jurisdiction over the listed colonies and reservations (Battle Mountain, Carson, Dresslerville, Elko, Goshute, Lovelock, Odger's Ranch, Reno-Sparks, Ruby Valley, South Fork, Washoe Tribal Farms, Washoe Pinenut, Winnemucca, Yomba, and Duckwater). (40 Fed. Reg. 27,501 (June 30, 1975).)
facts.locator: 40 Fed. Reg. at 27,501 (BIA notices, third column)
facts.quote: to retrocede to the United States of America all civil and criminal jurisdiction acquired by the State of Nevada
facts.note: The notices accept the offer of S.B. 491 (1973 Nev. Stat. ch. 601) for 14 listed areas and, in a second notice, Duckwater (S.B. 578, 1975 Nev. Stat. ch. 474), "effective on July 1, 1975 at 12:01 a.m., e.s.t." Roster mapping: Battle Mountain, Elko and South Fork to Te-Moak; Carson, Dresslerville, Washoe Tribal Farms and Pinenut to Washoe; "Goshute Reservation" to the Goshute Confederated Tribes (reservation also in Utah). Odger's Ranch and Ruby Valley Allotment not mapped.

facts.detail: The 1975 notice did not cover the Ely Colony; Nevada retroceded it later (Assembly Bill 702 of 1985), and the Department of the Interior accepted retrocession of all civil and criminal jurisdiction over the Ely Indian Colony in a notice published February 26, 1988. (53 Fed. Reg. 5837 (Feb. 26, 1988).)
facts.quote: retrocession to the United States of all jurisdiction, civil and criminal, over the Ely Indian Colony
facts.note: Already recorded by you; included to answer why the Ely colony is not in the 1975 notice. The 1976 AIPRC report (at 29) says Ely Colony was the one previously covered area that did not choose retrocession in the 1974 referendum ("exception of Ely Colony chose retrocession" is OCR text). The notice prints the effective date as "March 1,1987", which looks like a misprint of 1988; I could not confirm.

facts.detail: The Pyramid Lake Reservation was never under Nevada jurisdiction under the 1955 act: Washoe County petitioned and the Governor excluded it by proclamation of June 27, 1955, and the exclusion was never withdrawn. (Davis v. Warden, 88 Nev. 443, 446, 498 P.2d 1346 (1972).)
facts.quote: The Washoe County Board of Commissioners did petition the Governor to exclude the Pyramid Lake Indian Reservation from the operation of NRS 41.430, and the Governor, by proclamation, honored that petition on June 27, 1955.
facts.note: The court held state courts lacked jurisdiction over Pyramid Lake members' crimes on the reservation and vacated the convictions. Nevada Supreme Court, 1972.

facts.detail: The 1975 retrocession notice lists only the areas over which Nevada had acquired jurisdiction; Fallon, Walker River, Duck Valley, Fort McDermitt, Moapa, Las Vegas, Summit Lake, Yerington, Fort Mojave and Timbisha lands are not on it, and the notice does not say why. (40 Fed. Reg. 27,501.)
facts.quote: to retrocede to the United States of America all civil and criminal jurisdiction acquired by the State of Nevada
facts.note: INFERENCE, not stated in any source I read: because the notice covers only jurisdiction "acquired by the State," a nation absent from it was not under state jurisdiction in 1975. The 1976 AIPRC report (fn. 21) lists the previously covered areas and omits these nations. The 1955 act let counties exclude Indian country by Governor's proclamation (Pyramid Lake did); I did not locate the proclamations or minutes for the other counties, so the reason for each nation is unconfirmed. Fort Mojave also has AZ/CA lands; Duck Valley ID; Fort McDermitt OR.
